title: A Field Bought in a Doomed Land
sum: Jerusalem is under siege and Jeremiah is locked up in the palace courtyard for saying the city will fall. Then his cousin Hanamel comes and asks him to buy the family field at Anathoth, just as the LORD had said he would. Jeremiah buys it with all the proper paperwork, seals the deeds in a clay jar, and tells the bystanders, "Houses, fields and vineyards will be bought again in this land."

Then he prays. He praises the God who made everything and for whom nothing is "too wonderful," but he cannot hide his puzzlement: the city is about to be handed over, and yet he has been told to buy. The LORD answers in two parts. He confirms the judgment, with the sins listed again, and then promises a gathering, an everlasting covenant and a land where fields are bought and sold again. Judgment is certain and so is the return.
readings: Read as a sign act

Like the loincloth and the jar (chapters 13 and 19), the purchase is an act that carries the message. This one is a legal sale and a promise at once. Jeremiah must do it publicly, with witnesses, because the point is that people will see it and remember it.
Read as a prayer of doubt

The prayer (32:16–25) has the shape of a lament: praise, a recital of the past, a complaint ('and yet you, Lord GOD, said to me, Buy the field'). Many readers find that the chapter shows faith best when it is least sure of itself.

views.H: The year is 588/587 BC, the tenth of Zedekiah. The Babylonian army has taken most of Judah and holds the roads to Jerusalem; Lachish and Azekah are the last fortified towns (34:7). Jeremiah's cousin sells land in Benjamin, which the Babylonians control. The sale is a real transaction of its time, and keeping a deed in a clay jar so that it will last (32:14) fits the practice of the period.
views.C: Many scholars think the story of the purchase (32:6–15) belongs to the stories about Jeremiah that are often credited to Baruch, and that the prayer (32:16–25) and the long answer (32:26–44) were shaped later in the language of Deuteronomy, which is why the LORD's answer sounds like 31:31–34. The Greek has a shorter text throughout the chapter, and in 32:5, 32:11 and 32:17 the differences matter.
views.J: Radak reads the price differently from the Plain English Translation: the "shekels" are minas and the "silver" is selas, and he adds that Targum Jonathan translates it the same way (seven minin and ten selain). The Plain English Translation counts the Hebrew as seventeen shekels. The sale follows the land law of Leviticus 25, in which family land is redeemed and not lost for good.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 32:17 and 32:27 the voice of Genesis 18:14, Luke 1:37 and Matthew 19:26: nothing is impossible with God. Some read the everlasting covenant (32:40) with the new covenant of Hebrews 8; others point out that Jeremiah himself sets it in the land of Judah.
views.F: Futurist readers point to 32:37, the gathering from all the lands, as a promise still to come in full. Others read it as fulfilled in the return from Babylon under Persia, or in the church.

deep.b:
For this part the writer read these witnesses directly, verse by verse: the Hebrew of the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), word by word, with its Ketiv and Qere notes, in the STEPBible text; the Dead Sea scrolls that preserve these chapters, in the transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC), which for these seven chapters shows only 4QJer-c (4Q72), for parts of 33:16–20; and the Greek as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus (the chapters are 39 to 45 in Greek numbering). Ziegler's Göttingen edition was not read directly: where this part says "the Greek" it means Swete's Codex Vaticanus. The Targum of Jeremiah (Hayward's translation), the Vulgate and the Peshitta are reported from the studies named in each note. On Sefaria's text the writer read the Aramaic of Targum Jonathan at 33:15 and Radak at 32:9, 33:16, 33:24, 34:5 and 36:23.

The Greek of these chapters is shorter than the Hebrew by many small phrases ("the LORD declares," titles, repeated names, "the prophet," "king of Judah"). They are not listed one by one. Examples are 32:1, 32:3, 34:2 and 35:13. The variants name the places where the shortness changes the sense.

deep.h: Ketiv and Qere in chapters 32 to 38
deep.b: The Masoretes wrote some words one way and told the reader to say them another way (Ketiv, "what is written", and Qere, "what is read"). In these chapters the differences are spelling or grammar and do not change the sense of the Plain English Translation: 32:1 (year), 32:4 (eyes), 32:23 (law), 32:35 (cause to sin), 33:8 (all), 33:26 (I will turn back / I will bring back, which touches the idiom "turn their fortunes around" but is rendered the same either way), 34:11 (they subjugated), 34:17 (terror), 37:4 (prison), 37:19 (where), 38:2 (he will live), 38:11 (rags) and 38:16 (the Qere leaves out the object marker). The Plain English Translation follows the reading tradition in each case.

echoes: Jeremiah 31:31–34; Genesis 23; Leviticus 25:23–34; Ruth 4:1–12; Genesis 18:14; Deuteronomy 26:5–9; Deuteronomy 30:1–5; Ezekiel 11:19; 2 Kings 25:1–7; Luke 1:37

settings.what: Jeremiah's message that Zedekiah will be taken to Babylon, as the king quotes it
settings.to: Zedekiah and the court
settings.when: 588/587 BC, the tenth year of Zedekiah, with the Babylonian siege under way
settings.why: The message is the reason Jeremiah is in custody: the king locked him up for saying the city would fall and he himself would be taken. It was meant to warn the king and to be heard before it came true. It also shows that what follows, the purchase and the prayer, is a hope held by a man the king has silenced.
settings.readers: Exiles reading the book after 586 knew the prophecy had come true. Putting it first lets them hear the promise of return as the word of a prophet already proved right.

settings.what: The purchase of the field at Anathoth
settings.by: Jeremiah, in the first person, with the LORD's order
settings.to: Hanamel, the witnesses, Baruch and all the Judeans sitting in the courtyard of the guard
settings.when: in the tenth year of Zedekiah, in the palace courtyard, when the city is under siege
settings.why: The act is a sign. It shows publicly that the land will be bought and sold again in Judah. The witnesses and the signed deed make it a fact on record that survives the city's fall.
settings.readers: For the exiles it was a pledge that their fields still belonged to them. The deeds in the jar prove that the hope was made in the siege and not after it.

settings.what: Jeremiah's prayer
settings.to: The LORD, overheard by the reader
settings.when: just after the purchase, when the field is bought and the siege goes on
settings.why: Jeremiah brings his doubt to God: the LORD has told him to buy, and the Chaldeans have the city. The prayer does what a lament does, praising God and then stating the problem, so that the LORD can answer.
settings.readers: A pattern for exiles who also had to pray when God's word and their circumstances did not match.

settings.what: The LORD's answer: judgment and a promise
settings.to: Jeremiah, and through him the people of Jerusalem under siege
settings.when: after the prayer, in the same year
settings.why: To say that the siege and the purchase do not contradict each other. The city falls because of the people's long sin (32:30–35), and the LORD will still gather them, make an everlasting covenant and restore the land (32:36–44).
views: Many scholars see the Deuteronomic language of 32:17–23 and 32:36–41 as a later shaping of an older core.
Jeremiah spoke the whole answer in the siege, and the rich language comes from his own use of Deuteronomy.
settings.readers: The whole book ends on a note of survival (52:31–34), and this answer is where the book's promise to the exiles is first given in full.

title: Healing, a Branch and Two Covenants
sum: Jeremiah is still locked up when a second word comes, in a time when houses are being torn down to hold off the siege. The LORD invites him to call on him, and he will answer with great, hidden things. They are promises: healing for the city, forgiveness, a return of Judah and Israel, and a sound of weddings and thanksgiving in places that are now empty. Shepherds will again count their flocks in every region.

The second half (33:14–26) is not in the oldest Greek. It repeats the promise of a righteous Branch for David (compare 23:5–6) and then ties the royal line and the Levite priests to the LORD's covenant with day and night. The people say the LORD has thrown away the two families he chose. He answers that as long as day and night keep their order, he will not throw away the offspring of Jacob and David.
readings: Read as a message for the besieged

The first half (33:1–13) answers what the people in the city see: ruined houses, corpses, an empty land. The LORD does not deny it. He says the same place will hear the sound of the groom and the bride and a song of thanks.
Read as a later addition

Because the Greek lacks 33:14–26 and the passage repeats and expands 23:5–6, many scholars treat it as a later supplement that gave the book's hope a Davidic and priestly shape. Others think the Greek translator left it out, and point to the Qumran scroll that has part of it.

views.H: The siege is on (33:4–5). The promises of return, healing, weddings and flocks answer the loss that the city is suffering. After the exile ended in 539 BC, the returned exiles sang the song of 33:11 when they laid the foundation of the second temple (Ezra 3:11). No king of David's line sat on the throne in the Persian period.
views.C: The chapter is a test case for the two editions of Jeremiah. The Greek has 33:1–13 but not 33:14–26; the Qumran scroll 4QJer-c has words from 33:16–20. Scholars who think the Greek represents an earlier edition (Tov) read the passage as part of the later expansion of the Hebrew that became the Masoretic Text; those who think the Greek is shortened read it as original.
views.J: Radak reads the name in 33:16 as given to Jerusalem and connects it with the Messiah; the Targum has 'Messiah of righteousness' in 33:15. Radak takes the 'two clans' of 33:24 to be David's house and Aaron's. The Davidic and Levitical promises are part of the hope of the restoration of both kingship and the Temple service.
views.X: Christians have read the Branch as Jesus (Luke 1:78) and the Davidic promise as fulfilled in his everlasting kingdom (Luke 1:32–33). The promise of a Levitical priesthood forever is read in the church as met in Christ's priesthood (Hebrews 7), by some as a spiritual priesthood of all believers, and by others as still to be met literally. See the card below.
views.F: Some futurist readers (Dispensationalists) expect a literal Davidic king and a rebuilt temple with Levitical priests in the age to come. Others take the Branch to be Christ now reigning, and the 'priests' to be the church.

deep.b:
Greek chapter 40 ends where the Hebrew chapter 33 reaches verse 13. Verses 14 to 26 are therefore missing in Swete's Codex Vaticanus, and the critical edition of Ziegler agrees, as reported by Tov. The passage is one of the clearest cases in the book. Fragments of 33:16–20 survive in the Qumran scroll 4QJer-c (4Q72), which shares the longer text of the Masoretic tradition. In verses 17 and 18 the scroll differs from the Masoretic Text only in spelling; the other words in 16 to 20 that it holds are partly restored by its editors and are not cited as readings. The scroll proves that a Hebrew copy had the passage in the last centuries before Jesus. It does not show whether the Greek translator found it in his Hebrew copy.

Each of the thirteen verses has a variant entry, so a reader can switch the passage off and see the Greek's shorter chapter.

echoes: Jeremiah 23:5–6; Jeremiah 30:17; Jeremiah 31:35–37; Genesis 8:22; Genesis 15:5; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Numbers 25:11–13; Hebrews 7:11–28; Luke 1:32–33; Luke 1:78

settings.what: The word of healing and rebuilding
settings.to: Jeremiah in the courtyard, and through him the people in the besieged city
settings.when: a second word, soon after chapter 32, in the tenth year of Zedekiah
settings.why: To answer the siege's despair with a call to prayer and a list of what the LORD will do: heal, forgive, rebuild, restore joy and flocks.
settings.readers: Exiles who read this after 586 saw in the list what they had lost and what they were promised: weddings, thanksgiving songs in the temple, flocks in every region.

settings.what: The promise of the Branch and the unbroken line of David and the priests
settings.to: The people of Judah, in or after the siege
settings.when: in the siege, or (for critical readers) in the Persian period after the exile
settings.why: To say that the promise to David (2 Samuel 7) and to the Levite priests has not failed even though the throne and altar are about to be gone.
views: Spoken by Jeremiah in the courtyard, as a word of comfort that repeats and widens 23:5–6.
Added after the exile, when there was no king, to hold the hope for a king and for the temple service in the same covenant.
settings.readers: Readers in the Persian period, when there was a temple and no king, would hear the promise of a David's line and Levite priests as the promise of both institutions to come.

settings.what: The covenant with day and night, and the answer to those who say the LORD has rejected the two clans
settings.to: Jeremiah, and the people who say the LORD has rejected his chosen families
settings.when: after the promise of 33:14–18
settings.why: To answer despair in two steps: the LORD's covenant is as fixed as day and night, and the people who despise Israel are wrong.
settings.readers: For exiles who feared that the LORD had finished with Israel and David, these verses give the strongest answer in the book.

traditions.q: Are the promised Levitical priests and offerings (33:18, 21–22) to be met literally?
views: Fulfilled in Christ: the Catechism says that everything the priesthood of the Old Covenant prefigured finds its fulfillment in Christ, the one mediator, and that the ministerial priesthood shares in his priesthood (Catechism 1544–1547).

Fulfilled in Christ the priest and king and in the Church's liturgy: the Liturgy of St John Chrysostom calls Christ both the one who offers and the one who is offered, and the Church's bishops and priests serve in his priesthood.

The Levitical priesthood was a shadow that ended in Christ's once-for-all priesthood, which believers share as a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9); Calvin reads the promise in this way in his commentary on Jeremiah.

Still to come in a literal sense: the promise of David's throne and Levitical priests belongs to national Israel and will be met in the Messiah's kingdom, with a rebuilt temple in which sacrifices are memorials.

title: Release Promised, Release Cancelled
sum: Jeremiah brings Zedekiah the plain word: the city will burn and he himself will be captured and taken to Babylon, though he will die in peace. Lachish and Azekah are the only fortified towns Judah has left. Then the chapter turns to a different scene. In the middle of the siege Zedekiah and the people cut a covenant in the temple to free their Hebrew slaves, as the law of Moses commanded.

Then the slave owners changed their minds. The Babylonian army left for a time, and the owners took their slaves back. The LORD answers with a bitter play on words: you would not proclaim a release, so I proclaim a release for you, to the sword, disease and famine. The men who passed between the halves of a cut calf in their covenant will be treated like the calf.
readings: Read as a case of broken law

Exodus 21 and Deuteronomy 15 required the release of Hebrew slaves in the seventh year, and Judah had not kept it. The covenant of Zedekiah's day was a late and costly obedience, and the owners canceled it when it cost them.
Read as a case of repentance undone
The chapter is built around the word shuv. They turned and did what was right; they turned again. The people's repentance lasted as long as the danger did.

views.H: The siege began in January 588 (2 Kings 25:1). The release took place in the first stage, perhaps while the Egyptian army approached; when the Babylonians went away (34:21; 37:5), the owners took their slaves back. Lachish Letter 4 may describe Azekah's fall in these same months.
views.C: The chapter is prose in the language of Deuteronomy, and many scholars, such as Nicholson, assign such prose sermons to Deuteronomistic editors. The Greek lacks the cutting of the calf and the passing between the pieces (34:18–19), and has 'six years' for 'seven' in 34:14. The slave release itself, as an event, is widely accepted as historical.
views.J: Radak reads 'you will die in peace' (34:5) as meaning a natural death on his bed with royal honors, and adds the saying of the Sages that Nebuchadnezzar died during Zedekiah's lifetime. The law of release is read in Jewish tradition with the sabbatical year and Jubilee.
views.X: The chapter has been read as a warning that obedience to God that stops when it costs something is not obedience. It is cited in sermons on freeing the oppressed (Isaiah 58:6; Luke 4:18).
views.F: For futurists the chapter has little direct role. Those who read the covenant sacrifice of Genesis 15 as the pattern of the new covenant see in the cut calf here the curse that falls on covenant-breakers.

deep.b: The rite behind 34:18–19 is the oath-sacrifice of Genesis 15. The Aramaic Sefire treaty has the same self-curse: "Just as this calf is cut in two, so may Mati'el be cut in two." In Jeremiah the rite is performed by people who then break their promise. The LORD's treatment of them is exactly what the rite said would happen to a covenant-breaker. The Greek (Swete) gives a much shorter text without the cutting.

echoes: Genesis 15:9–18; Exodus 21:2–6; Deuteronomy 15:12–18; Leviticus 25:39–46; Jeremiah 37:5–11; Isaiah 58:6; 2 Kings 25:1–7

settings.what: The message to Zedekiah
settings.to: Zedekiah king of Judah, in Jerusalem
settings.when: in the siege, 588/587 BC, when only Lachish and Azekah still held
settings.why: To tell the king plainly that the city will fall and he will be taken, and to give him the one comfort he has: he will not die by the sword. It also invites him to hear the word of the LORD (34:4).
settings.readers: Exiles reading it later saw that every word came true, and that Zedekiah had been warned.

settings.what: The sermon on the freed slaves
settings.to: Zedekiah, the officials, the priests and the slave owners of Jerusalem
settings.when: after the slaves were taken back, during the pause in the siege (34:21)
settings.why: To condemn a broken oath made in the temple. The slave owners had done right and then undone it; the LORD turns the word 'release' on them.
settings.readers: Exiles would take it as one more reason for the fall of Jerusalem: not only idols but injustice to their own people.
views: It was the seventh-year release under pressure of the siege (Sarna), a plan to gain soldiers, or a wish to win God's favor.

title: The Family That Kept Its Word
sum: In the days of Jehoiakim, Jeremiah brings the whole clan of the Rechabites into a room of the temple, sets out bowls of wine and cups, and says, "Drink." They refuse. Their ancestor Jonadab son of Rechab ordered them never to drink wine, build houses, sow seed or plant vineyards, and for more than two centuries the family has lived in tents. They are in Jerusalem only because the Babylonian army drove them in from the countryside.

The LORD uses them as a lesson. A family keeps the command of a human ancestor who spoke once, and Judah will not listen to God, who has spoken to them over and over. The Rechabites are promised that the family will never lack a man to stand before him.
readings: Read as a sermon in action
Jeremiah does not tell the Rechabites to do anything new. The test is staged to show the people the contrast, and the Rechabites are an unwitting example.
Read as a story of family loyalty

The Rechabites are praised for faithfulness to a rule that was their own, not God's law. Some readers admire the loyalty without taking the specific rules (no wine, no houses) as commands for everyone.

views.H: The scene is set about 599–598 BC, when Babylonian and allied raiders moved through Judah (2 Kings 24:1–2) and country people took refuge in Jerusalem. The Rechabites go back to Jonadab, who aided Jehu about 841 BC (2 Kings 10:15–23).
views.C: The chapter is prose in the Deuteronomic style and is placed out of order, before the events of chapter 34 (Zedekiah's reign). Scholars have debated whether its point is the contrast with Judah or a story about the Rechabites themselves, and whether the Rechabites were a religious order, a nomadic guild or a clan.
views.J: 'Stand before me' is the language of service to God (Deuteronomy 10:8, of the Levites), and it has been read as a promise that the Rechabites would always have worshipers in God's service.
views.X: Christian readers have used the chapter to argue for total abstinence from wine, which the text itself does not say, and as an image of faithful obedience that Christians owe to Christ.
views.F: The chapter has no direct role in futurist readings. Its promise to the Rechabites is read in some Bibles as a promise to the faithful remnant.

echoes: 2 Kings 10:15–23; 1 Chronicles 2:55; Numbers 6:1–4; Amos 2:11–12; Deuteronomy 10:8; Jeremiah 34:8–22; Nehemiah 3:14

settings.what: The Rechabites and the wine
settings.by: Jeremiah, in the first person, on the LORD's order
settings.to: The Rechabites, in a room of the temple
settings.when: in the days of Jehoiakim (609–598 BC), after the Babylonian raids drove them into Jerusalem
settings.why: To stage a test of obedience before witnesses. They pass it, and the test becomes the example that follows.
settings.readers: Exiles reading it saw that a small family could keep a command for generations in a hard life, and so Judah's failure to listen to God was not for lack of an example.

settings.what: The LORD's charge against Judah
settings.to: The men of Judah and the people of Jerusalem
settings.when: after the scene with the Rechabites
settings.why: To make the contrast clear: the Rechabites listened to a human ancestor; Judah has not listened to God, who sent his servants the prophets again and again.
settings.readers: The exiles are told why the calamity came.

settings.what: The promise to the Rechabites
settings.to: The house of the Rechabites
settings.when: at the end of the scene in the temple room
settings.why: To reward their faithfulness with a promise to their family.
settings.readers: A promise that would be read after the fall as a sign that faithfulness is never forgotten.

title: The Scroll the King Burned
sum: In 605 BC the LORD tells Jeremiah to write down everything he has said since the days of Josiah, in the hope that Judah will hear and turn. Jeremiah dictates, and his scribe Baruch writes. Because Jeremiah is barred from the temple, Baruch reads the scroll aloud there, on a fast day in the ninth month of the following year. The officials who hear it are afraid, tell Baruch to hide with Jeremiah, and report the scroll to the king.

The king, Jehoiakim, sits by a fire in the winter house while the scroll is read. Each time Jehudi finishes three or four columns, the king cuts them off with a knife and throws them on the fire, until the whole scroll is gone. He and his servants do not tear their clothes. The LORD hides Jeremiah and Baruch, tells Jeremiah to write another scroll, and sentences Jehoiakim. The new scroll has the same words and many more.
readings: Read as the story of the book's beginning

The chapter is the book's own account of how it came to be written: dictated, read, burned, rewritten and enlarged. Whatever the first scroll held, the story says that the book of Jeremiah is a book that survived a king's attempt to destroy it.
Read as a contrast with Josiah
In 2 Kings 22 the king hears a book read, tears his clothes and repents. Here the king hears a book read, cuts it up and burns it. The same families are present in both scenes.

views.H: Dates: the fourth year of Jehoiakim is 605 BC, the year of Carchemish. The reading is in the ninth month of the fifth year, December 604. The Babylonian Chronicle says Nebuchadnezzar took Ashkelon in that month. Seal impressions from Jerusalem name some of the people in the story, such as Gemariah son of Shaphan; the Baruch bulla is unprovenanced, and a 2014 laboratory study argued that it is modern (a 2016 reply disputes this).
views.C: The chapter is a key text for how Jeremiah was made: the first scroll, the second and enlarged scroll (36:32), and the role of Baruch. Scholars differ on what the first scroll held and whether the story is historical in detail. The Greek has the eighth year for the fifth in 36:9 and in 36:25 a reversed sense: two officials urge the king to burn the scroll (see the variants).
views.J: Radak says delatot, 'doors', means the pages of the scroll, and notes that the Targum renders it as 'pieces.' Jewish tradition credits Jeremiah with writing his own book (Bava Batra 15a). Radak also repeats the Sages' story that Jehoiakim, shown Jeremiah's Lamentations, answered each verse by claiming kingship for himself and, at the line "The LORD has given her sorrow" (Lamentations 1:5), cut out all the divine names in it and burned them.
views.X: Christian readers have seen the chapter as a lesson about the endurance of the word of God (Isaiah 40:8; Matthew 24:35). The tearing of clothes by Josiah and not by Jehoiakim is a common sermon contrast.
views.F: Futurists do not draw much on the chapter. Its prophecies of Jehoiakim's end and the coming of Babylon were fulfilled in history.

deep.b: Two clay seal impressions bear on the chapter. Nahman Avigad published one reading "Belonging to Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe" in 1978; it came from the antiquities market, with no find spot, and its authenticity is disputed (Goren and Arie argued in 2014 that the impressions are modern; van der Veen, Deutsch and Barkay replied in 2016). The other, "Gemaryahu son of Shaphan," was excavated in the City of David in 1982 in a layer burned in 586, as reported by Yigal Shiloh. Together with the excavated impressions of Jehucal and Gedaliah (38:1), the Gemariah impression shows the officials of the book in the real administration of the city. None of them shows what was in the scroll.

echoes: 2 Kings 22:3–20; Exodus 34:1; Isaiah 40:8; Jeremiah 25:1–14; Jeremiah 26:20–24; Jeremiah 45:1; Jeremiah 51:59–64; Matthew 24:35

settings.what: The order to write the scroll and to have it read
settings.by: The LORD to Jeremiah; Jeremiah to Baruch
settings.to: Jeremiah, then Baruch the scribe
settings.when: 605 BC, the fourth year of Jehoiakim, with Babylon rising after Carchemish
settings.why: To give Judah one more chance, in writing, to hear the whole message before disaster. The words were first spoken to be heard; written down, they could be read where Jeremiah was barred from going.
views: The scroll held the oracles Jeremiah had spoken since 627.
What the first scroll held cannot be recovered; it may have been a core of the poems.
settings.readers: The exiles and later readers knew the scroll as the origin of the book. It told them the book had been through a king's fire.

settings.what: The public reading on a fast day, and the report to the officials
settings.to: All the people gathered in the temple for the fast; then Micaiah, who reported it, and the officials in the scribe's room
settings.when: the ninth month of the fifth year of Jehoiakim (December 604 BC)
settings.why: To put the LORD's warning in front of the whole people at the moment they were fasting, and to get it to the court. The officials act at once: they understand its danger, and they send Baruch and Jeremiah into hiding.
settings.readers: Readers see an official class split: some respect the word, and the king burns it.

settings.what: The reading before the king and the burning
settings.to: Jehoiakim and his officials in the winter house
settings.when: the same ninth month
settings.why: The scene shows what a king does with a word he will not hear. The reading is the last warning, and the king's answer is final.
settings.readers: For exiles it explains why the king and the kingdom fell.

settings.what: The new scroll and the sentence on Jehoiakim
settings.to: Jeremiah, Baruch and Jehoiakim
settings.when: after the burning
settings.why: To show that the word cannot be destroyed, and to give the king his sentence.
settings.readers: Later readers had the longer scroll in their hands, and the verse says so.

title: A Prophet Arrested at the Gate
sum: Zedekiah is on the throne, but neither he nor his servants listen to the LORD's words through Jeremiah. He sends two men to ask Jeremiah to pray for the city. Pharaoh's army has come out of Egypt, and the Babylonians have pulled back from Jerusalem. Jeremiah's answer is that the Egyptians will go home, the Chaldeans will come back, and the city will burn. Even if Judah beat the whole Babylonian army, the wounded would rise and burn it.

While the siege is lifted, Jeremiah starts for his family land in Benjamin. At the Benjamin Gate a captain arrests him for deserting to the enemy. The officials beat him and put him in a scribe's house turned into a prison. After many days the king sends for him secretly and asks if there is a word from the LORD. Jeremiah says there is: you will be handed over to the king of Babylon. He begs not to be sent back to that house, and the king puts him in the courtyard of the guard with a daily loaf of bread.
readings: Read as a political drama
The chapter shows a weak king caught between his officials and a prophet he fears and respects, and it shows how any word about surrender could be taken as treason.
Read as the story of a rejected prophet
Jeremiah is the one whose words come true and who is jailed for saying them. The question 'Where are your prophets?' (37:19) is the climax.

views.H: Pharaoh Hophra's army marched north about 588/587, the Babylonians lifted the siege for a time, and then returned. The chapter sets this at the centre of the siege (37:5, 11). Lachish Letter 3 says a Judean commander went down to Egypt, which fits Zedekiah's search for Egyptian help.
views.C: Scholars often assign this chapter and 38 to the Baruch narrative, with two accounts of Jeremiah's arrest and his meetings with Zedekiah. Some think 37:11–21 and 38:14–28 are two versions of one story, since each has the secret meeting and the plea not to be returned to the house of Jonathan. Others hold them to be two separate events. The Greek differs in small ways, including 'to buy' for 'to claim a share' in 37:12.
views.J: Jewish tradition honors Jeremiah as the prophet of the destruction mourned on the Ninth of Av, and the scenes of his arrest and imprisonment are part of how that tradition remembers him.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Jeremiah a figure of the suffering prophet whom the authorities beat and imprison for unwelcome truth, and have compared him to Christ's trial.
views.F: Futurists do not use the chapter directly.

echoes: Jeremiah 21:1–10; Jeremiah 7:16; Jeremiah 14:11; Jeremiah 15:1; Jeremiah 38:14–28; Ezekiel 17:15–17; Deuteronomy 18:21–22; 2 Kings 24:17

settings.what: The king's request for prayer and the LORD's answer
settings.by: Zedekiah's envoys Jehucal and Zephaniah; the LORD, through Jeremiah
settings.to: Jeremiah; then, through the envoys, the king of Judah
settings.when: in the siege, when the Babylonians have pulled back to meet Pharaoh's army (about 588/587 BC)
settings.why: The king wants hope that the lifting of the siege is God's answer. The LORD gives him the opposite: the army that came to help will go home, and the city will be burned.
settings.readers: Exiles recalled that Jeremiah had told the king the Egyptians would fail, and they had.

settings.what: Jeremiah's arrest at the Benjamin Gate and his imprisonment
settings.by: Irijah the guard captain and the officials; Jeremiah answers "A lie!"
settings.to: Jeremiah, in the gate and then before the officials
settings.when: while the Babylonian army has pulled away from Jerusalem because of Pharaoh's army (37:11), about 588/587 BC
settings.why: Anyone leaving the city toward the enemy's side could be taken for a deserter, and Jeremiah's message made him an easy suspect. The officials, furious at him, put him in a house made into a prison. The text gives Jeremiah's own denial ("A lie!") and no more of his reasons.
settings.readers: Exiles who read this knew that the prophet who said the city would fall was jailed as a traitor, and that he was not.

settings.what: Jeremiah's secret meeting with the king
settings.to: Each other, in the king's house
settings.when: after Jeremiah's arrest and many days in the cells
settings.why: The king asks privately for a word because he cannot ask in public. Jeremiah answers the same as before, then asks for justice and mercy for himself.
settings.readers: It shows the king's weakness and the prophet's boldness.

title: Down into the Mud, Up by the Cushite
sum: Four officials hear Jeremiah telling people that whoever stays in the city will die, and whoever goes out to the Chaldeans will live. They tell the king that the man is weakening the soldiers and must die. Zedekiah says, "He is in your hands," and they lower Jeremiah by ropes into a cistern with no water but a deep layer of mud.

Ebed-melech, a Cushite court official, tells the king what has been done. The king orders him to take thirty men and pull Jeremiah out. Ebed-melech lowers rags for padding so the ropes will not cut him. Then the king asks Jeremiah privately for the truth. Jeremiah says: surrender and you will live; refuse and the city will burn and your women will mock you with a taunt song. The king is afraid of the Judeans who have gone over to the enemy and of his own officials, and asks Jeremiah to keep the meeting secret. Jeremiah stays in the courtyard of the guard until the city is captured.
readings: Read as a history of the last days
The chapter shows the weakness of the king and the power of the officials, and what Jeremiah's advice looked like to the men who had to defend the city.
Read as a contrast of characters

Zedekiah has power and cannot act. The officials act and do evil. Ebed-melech, a foreigner and a court official without rank in the council, acts in the right way. Jeremiah stands among them and does not change his message.

views.H: The events fall late in the siege, in the summer of 586 BC. The Lachish letters speak of officials who weaken the hands of the army (Letter 6), and the seal impressions of Jehucal and Gedaliah son of Pashhur are reported from the City of David. The prophecy to Zedekiah's household is fulfilled in 39:4–7 and 52:7–11.
views.C: Many scholars give chapters 37 and 38 to the Baruch narrative. Some read 38:14–28 as a second account of the same meeting as 37:17–21. The Greek has several differences, such as three officials instead of four (38:1), no 'by disease' in 38:2, no 'court official' in 38:7 and a different accusation in 38:9.
views.J: Jewish tradition holds that Jeremiah wrote Lamentations (Bava Batra 15a), which has led readers to hear this scene in Lamentations 3:53–55. Ebed-melech's reward is told in 39:15–18.
views.X: Ebed-melech is remembered as an early foreigner who showed mercy to a prophet. Some Christian preachers set Jeremiah's descent into the pit beside Joseph and Christ, and Ebed-melech beside the faithful outsider in the Gospels.
views.F: Futurists do not use the chapter directly.

echoes: Jeremiah 21:8–10; Jeremiah 37:3–21; Jeremiah 39:15–18; Genesis 37:24; Psalm 69:2; Lamentations 3:53–55; Isaiah 56:3–5; Obadiah 7

settings.what: Jeremiah's call to surrender and the officials' reply
settings.by: Jeremiah, speaking to the people; the officials, speaking to the king
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem, then the king
settings.when: late in the siege, 587/586 BC
settings.why: Jeremiah tells the people the one way to live: go out to the Chaldeans. The officials hear it as treason in a war, since it weakens the soldiers.
views: Surrender is the way of life.
settings.readers: Later readers know Jeremiah was right and that the officials were not wrong that his words did weaken the city's will to fight.

settings.what: Ebed-melech's plea and the rescue
settings.by: Ebed-melech the Cushite, and King Zedekiah
settings.to: The king, at the Benjamin Gate
settings.when: after the officials threw Jeremiah into the cistern; the text does not say how soon
settings.why: To tell the king what the officials have done and to bring about the rescue.
settings.readers: Readers see a foreigner doing what Judah's leaders would not.

settings.what: The secret meeting with Zedekiah
settings.to: Each other, at the third entrance of the temple
settings.when: after the rescue, late in the siege
settings.why: The king asks for the truth, swears an oath to keep Jeremiah alive and then hears the same answer as before, with a clearer choice: go out and live, or stay and see the city burn and your women mock you.
settings.readers: The exiles who read this knew he did not go out, and that his house was taken out as Jeremiah said.
